title: Interfacial Faraday instability driven by interspecies-interaction modulation in a phase-separated binary Bose-Einstein condensate
abstract: We investigate interfacial Faraday instabilities in a quasi-two-dimensional, phase-separated binary Bose-Einstein condensate driven by periodic modulation of the interspecies scattering length. In the strongly immiscible regime, the interspecies interaction energy is concentrated near the internal interface, linking the modulation to interfacial tension and the capillary restoring force. We quantify the first-order tension response through its logarithmic sensitivity and account for nonlinear tension variations at finite modulation amplitudes. A sharp-interface capillary model and Floquet analysis yield discrete azimuthal-mode frequencies and primary instability tongues that shift toward higher driving frequencies with increasing mode order. Gross-Pitaevskii simulations reveal star-shaped interface patterns with threefold to eightfold rotational symmetry. The eightfold mode exhibits subharmonic oscillations and approximately exponential growth of its period-averaged amplitude over a small-deformation interval. These results provide a route to frequency-selective excitation of interfacial capillary modes through interspecies-interaction control.
summary: This paper analyzes how modulating the interspecies interaction in a phase-separated binary BEC drives interfacial Faraday instabilities. By combining theoretical Floquet analysis with full Gross-Pitaevskii simulations, the authors predict specific resonance conditions for exciting capillary modes. The key finding is the demonstration of preferential, exponentially growing excitation of the eightfold interface pattern, offering a route for frequency-selective control over quantum fluid interfaces.
main_problem: The study investigates interfacial Faraday instabilities in a phase-separated binary Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) when driven by periodic modulation of the interspecies scattering length.
main_result: The analysis predicts discrete azimuthal-mode frequencies and instability tongues, showing that the eightfold mode exhibits subharmonic oscillations and exponential growth of its amplitude, enabling frequency-selective excitation of capillary modes.
method: The research combines a sharp-interface capillary model with Floquet analysis to derive governing equations for the interface displacement, which are then validated and extended using full Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) simulations.
model_or_system: The system is a quasi-two-dimensional, phase-separated binary BEC (e.g., Rb-Rb) whose dynamics are governed by coupled 2D Gross-Pitaevskii equations. The driving mechanism is the time-periodic modulation of the interspecies scattering length, which modulates the interfacial tension.
key_observables: Interfacial tension ($\sigma$), azimuthal-mode frequencies ($m=3-8$), instability tongues, and the exponential growth rate ($\Gamma_{eff}$) of the eightfold mode amplitude.
important_parameters: Strongly immiscible regime ($K > 1$), modulation amplitude ($\epsilon_{AB}$), and the driving frequency ($\omega_D$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the planar-interface approximation for the interfacial tension ($\sigma$), although full GP simulations are used to test this approximation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the equilibrium density profiles and the time evolution of the normalized interfacial tension ($\sigma/\sigma_0$) under modulation. Later figures show the theoretical prediction of Floquet amplitude growth rates for the eightfold mode and the raw/averaged interface amplitudes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the microscopic link between scattering length modulation and time-dependent interfacial tension, to deriving the linearized Mathieu/Hill equation for interface modes, and finally performing full GP simulations to confirm parametric resonance and observe the characteristic subharmonic growth of the eightfold mode.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, controllable mechanism (tuning interspecies interactions) to excite specific, high-order capillary modes at the interface of a quantum fluid, which is highly relevant for controlling superfluid dynamics and pattern formation in BECs.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Equilibrium interface and density distributions in a phase-separated quasi-2D binary BEC. (a) Schematic of the disk–annulus configuration, with component B occupying the central disk and component A the surrounding annulus. Their common boundary is the internal A–B interface. (b,c) Equilibrium 2D density distributions of components A (87Rb) and B (85Rb), respectively, obtained from the stationary GP equations. (d) Radial density profiles nA(r) (blue solid line) and nB(r) (orange dashed line). The vertical dotted line marks the equilibrium interface radius R0.

FIG. 2. Interaction dependence and periodic modulation of the interfacial tension. (a) Normalized interfacial tension σ/σ0 as a function of the interspecies scattering length aAB. The open circle marks the reference point aAB = 426a0, where the loga- rithmic tension sensitivity is ΛAB = 0.2447. (b) Normalized interfacial tension σ(t)/σ0 over one driving period TD for a relative modulation amplitude ϵAB = 168/426 ≃0.3944. Both curves are calculated using the unexpanded tension function at fixed reference pressure and healing lengths.

FIG. 3. Free oscillation of the eightfold interface mode at con- stant aAB = 426a0. (a) Phase-sensitive eightfold interface dis- placement X8(t) obtained from the GP evolution. (b) Fourier amplitude spectrum normalized by its maximum. The gray dashed line marks the capillary prediction f8 = 47.8757 Hz, and the orange dotted line marks the frequency obtained from the free GP oscillation, 48.56 Hz.

FIG. 4. Primary Floquet instability tongues for interfacial modes m = 3–8, plotted against driving frequency fD and relative modulation amplitude ϵAB of aAB. The orange regions show the predictions of the capillary model. Open circles mark GP driving parameters at ϵAB = 168/426. The inset shows the theoretical Floquet amplitude growth rate Γ8 as a function of fD at ϵAB = 168/426 ≃0.3944. The open square marks its maximum, and the filled circle marks its value at fD = 95.7513 Hz.

FIG. 5. Star-shaped deformations of the internal A–B interface with azimuthal orders m = 3–8. The driving frequencies from left to right are fD = 21.19, 32.46, 47.15, 62.20, 78.59, 97.16 Hz. All snapshots use the reference scattering length aAB = 426a0 and modulation amplitude ∆aAB = 168a0. The two components exhibit complementary deformations of their common internal interface.
